Family Health

Lower left abdominal pain: periods, ovaries and other possible causes

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Lower abdominal pain can come from several nearby organs. Its side alone cannot identify the cause; how it starts, accompanying symptoms and the possibility of pregnancy determine the next step.

Location is a clue, but it does not identify the organ

Pain low on the left side of the abdomen may come from a reproductive organ, the bowel, the urinary tract or the abdominal wall. Similar conditions can also cause pain on the right or across the pelvis. The sensation may be cramping, sharp, heavy or burning, and some pain travels away from its starting point. You cannot identify an ovarian problem simply by pointing to one side.

Timing and accompanying symptoms matter. Note whether pain relates to a period, sex, eating, urination or passing stool, and whether it started suddenly or has gradually worsened. Pregnancy possibility, previous surgery, infections and fertility treatment are also useful context. Common causes include menstrual cramps, constipation and urinary infections, but a familiar location does not make a new severe episode safe to ignore.

Choose urgent care before trying to name the cause

Seek emergency help for sudden severe or rapidly worsening pain, collapse or faintness, shoulder-tip pain, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding, or signs of shock such as cold clammy skin, rapid breathing and marked weakness. Severe one-sided pain with vomiting can also require emergency assessment. If you feel faint or very unwell, do not drive yourself.

Get prompt medical advice for pelvic pain with fever, unusual discharge or bleeding, painful urination, persistent vomiting, or possible pregnancy. You do not need to have every symptom in a checklist. Persistent or recurrent pain that interferes with daily activities also deserves an appointment even if it is less severe. Emergency departments and primary-care teams can begin assessment; you do not always need to wait for a gynaecology appointment.

Menstrual cramps should not be dismissed when they change

Period pain, or dysmenorrhoea, commonly begins shortly before or around the start of bleeding as the uterus contracts. It can spread into the back or thighs and vary from a mild ache to stronger cramps. A warm compress used safely, gentle movement and an appropriate pain medicine may help a familiar mild pattern.

Arrange a review if pain stops you doing normal activities, becomes progressively worse, starts after years of relatively comfortable periods or is accompanied by heavy or irregular bleeding. Pain during sex, urination or bowel movements is also worth reporting. These are reasons to ask for help at any age, rather than only after 25. Severe or unusual pain should not be assumed to be ordinary cramps just because a period is due.

Endometriosis can affect more than period days

Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing elsewhere, often within the pelvis. It can cause painful periods, ongoing pelvic discomfort, pain during or after sex, and pain when passing urine or stool. Heavy bleeding and spotting between periods should also be discussed, although they have other possible causes and do not establish endometriosis.

The exact cause is not fully understood. Tell the clinician how symptoms affect work, sleep, relationships and daily activities, including symptoms outside menstruation. Examination and imaging may be part of the assessment, and further specialist investigation is sometimes needed. Treatment may involve pain management, hormonal treatment or surgery according to the findings and your plans for pregnancy. There is no need to accept disabling pain as an unavoidable part of having periods.

Most ovarian cysts are uncomplicated, but some cause pain

An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac in or on an ovary. Many functional cysts develop during the menstrual cycle, cause no symptoms and disappear over the following months. A cyst found on a scan is therefore not automatically dangerous or the explanation for every symptom. Follow-up depends on its appearance, size, your age and how you feel.

A larger cyst may cause pressure, bloating, pelvic discomfort or a frequent need to urinate. Rupture can cause sudden pain and sometimes internal bleeding. Sudden severe pain, especially with vomiting, fever, faintness or weakness, needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a scheduled repeat scan when the symptoms change sharply. Treatment may range from monitoring to surgery, depending on the particular complication.

Ovarian torsion is a time-sensitive possibility

Torsion occurs when an ovary, a fallopian tube or both twist around their supporting tissues, restricting blood flow. A cyst or an enlarged ovary can increase the risk, including in some pregnancies or during fertility treatment, but torsion can also happen without a known cyst. It is not limited to one side or exclusively to adults of reproductive age.

A common presentation is sudden one-sided pain with nausea or vomiting. Pain may come and go if twisting is intermittent, so temporary relief does not safely rule it out. The team may use ultrasound, but a blood-flow result alone cannot exclude torsion. Surgery may be needed to inspect and untwist the tissues promptly. Preserving the ovary is an important aim where possible; removal is not an automatic outcome, particularly in younger patients.

Consider ectopic pregnancy when pregnancy is possible

An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube. Symptoms may be absent early on or include one-sided lower abdominal pain, a missed period, unusual vaginal bleeding, watery brown bleeding or discomfort when passing urine or stool. These symptoms overlap with other problems. They need assessment rather than a diagnosis based on symptoms alone.

A correctly timed negative pregnancy test makes an ectopic pregnancy much less likely, but an early home test may need repeating. Do not let a test result delay care for severe pain, faintness or shoulder-tip pain. A positive test with no pregnancy seen on ultrasound is called a pregnancy of unknown location; it can mean a very early uterine pregnancy, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy. Follow-up blood tests and scans help clarify which applies.

A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency

If an ectopic pregnancy ruptures, internal bleeding can cause severe abdominal pain, dizziness, collapse, pallor or cold clammy skin. Shoulder-tip pain can be a sign of blood irritating the diaphragm. Call for emergency help if these symptoms occur, even if you did not know you were pregnant. Waiting for bleeding to become visible is unsafe because blood may be collecting inside the abdomen.

A rupture requires urgent treatment, commonly emergency surgery, and a damaged fallopian tube may need removal. Earlier diagnosed ectopic pregnancies may have other management options, depending on symptoms, scan findings and hormone levels. The correct approach cannot be chosen at home, and ongoing follow-up is essential when the pregnancy location or response to treatment is not yet clear.

Pelvic inflammatory disease can be subtle

Pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, is infection involving the upper reproductive tract. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are important causes, but organisms that are not sexually transmitted can also contribute. Some people have mild symptoms or very few, so the absence of severe pain or fever does not exclude infection.

Possible symptoms include lower abdominal pain, fever, unusual or unpleasant-smelling discharge, pain or bleeding during sex, burning when urinating and bleeding between periods. Seek assessment for these symptoms or possible STI exposure. Treatment often involves antibiotics, and recent partners may need testing and treatment. Complete the prescribed course and follow advice about avoiding sex until treatment is complete. Prompt care helps reduce complications, although antibiotics cannot reverse damage already present.

A groin hernia can affect women too

An inguinal hernia occurs when tissue, such as fat or part of the bowel, pushes through a weak area near the groin. It is more common in men, but it is not a male-only condition. You may notice a bulge that becomes more obvious with coughing, lifting or straining and smaller when lying down. Aching, heaviness or burning can occur; in someone with a scrotum, swelling may extend there.

A painful, firm or increasingly tender lump, skin colour change, vomiting, fever, abdominal swelling or inability to pass stool or gas can indicate trapped tissue or obstruction. Seek urgent emergency assessment and do not force a painful lump back yourself. If there is no emergency feature, arrange an examination to confirm the diagnosis and discuss treatment. Bowel or urinary causes of lower abdominal pain may need a different plan, so avoid assuming every pelvic symptom is gynaecological.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Severe or worsening pelvic pain, collapse or possible internal bleeding requires urgent assessment.

Period pain that disrupts life deserves review at any age.

Torsion, ectopic pregnancy and PID cannot be safely ruled out by a symptom checklist at home.

How BeMama can help

Record the onset, side, cycle timing and accompanying symptoms. Mention pregnancy possibility and fertility treatment early, and use urgent care when the symptoms warrant it.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for severe pain with faintness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, breathing difficulty or signs of shock. Sudden one-sided pain with vomiting also needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pain on the left is not automatically an ovarian problem.
  • Changed or disabling menstrual pain deserves attention.
  • A positive test with an empty early scan needs follow-up, not an automatic diagnosis.
  • Groin hernias can occur in women as well as men.

Frequently asked questions

Can these causes also produce right-sided pain?

Yes. Several can affect either side or the wider pelvis. Location alone is not diagnostic.

Should I wait until I am over 25 to report worsening cramps?

No. Disabling, progressive or changed period pain should be assessed at any age.

Does pain outside my period rule out endometriosis?

No. Endometriosis can also cause symptoms between periods, during sex or with bowel and bladder activity.

Does every ovarian cyst need surgery?

No. Many functional cysts settle without surgery, but follow-up and treatment depend on their features and your symptoms.

Can torsion pain come and go?

Yes. Intermittent pain does not safely exclude it, especially when sudden pain is accompanied by nausea or vomiting.

Does normal blood flow on a scan rule out torsion?

No. Doppler flow alone cannot rule it out. Clinicians consider the full picture and may need surgery to confirm and treat it.

Does an empty early scan prove an ectopic pregnancy?

No. With a positive pregnancy test it is a pregnancy of unknown location until follow-up clarifies whether it is early, miscarried or ectopic.

Can I ignore severe pain after a negative pregnancy test?

No. A negative result makes ectopic pregnancy less likely but does not make severe pain safe. Early tests and other urgent causes must be considered.

Does PID always cause high fever?

No. Symptoms may be mild or absent. Pelvic pain, unusual discharge, bleeding or possible exposure deserves assessment.

Are inguinal hernias only a problem for men?

No. Women can have them too. A painful firm lump with vomiting or inability to pass stool or gas needs emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
